docs.title: GNSS signals, generated on a GPU
docs.text:
A software GNSS simulator for receiver and anti-jam development. It renders phase-coherent baseband IQ for every satellite, every band and every antenna element, with jammers in the same scene, and writes files that any software or hardware receiver can use.

Get started Deploy a server How it works

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
• Multi-constellation, multi-band

    All visible satellites from a RINEX broadcast file, on every enabled band at once. Bands that share a carrier, such as GPS L1 and Galileo E1, are summed into one stream.

  • Antenna arrays

    M independent, phase-coherent IQ streams. Each element has a body-frame lever arm, an orientation and a radiation pattern (built-in polarisations or CST exports). Built for CRPA and null-steering work.

  • 6-DoF dynamics

    The receiver follows a piecewise-cubic trajectory: position, velocity, acceleration and jerk, plus the same for attitude, so each element's lever arm moves with it. A static receiver is a single latitude, longitude and altitude.

  • Interference in the same scene

    CW, triangle-FM and BPSK jammers, each with its own location, transmit power, carrier and antenna pattern. Path loss is applied, and each jammer is delayed per element, so the array sees where every one of them is.

  • Physics-based channel

    Light-time solution with Sagnac correction, broadcast satellite clocks, Saastamoinen troposphere with the Niell mapping function, and Klobuchar ionosphere scaled by 1/f² per band.

  • Exact code timing

    Every signal is band-limited to the sample rate before it is delayed. Code timing is exact at any rate, integer or fractional, and was confirmed by an independent signal analyser.

  • Ground truth on request

    The server can return the range, range rate, Doppler, delay and look angles that it actually generated for a satellite, so you can score a receiver against it.

  • Real navigation data

    Each signal carries its own message (LNAV, CNAV, I/NAV, B-CNAV1, D1/D2, GLONASS strings), encoded from the broadcast ephemeris with the ICD's parity, CRC and FEC, so receivers can decode it.

  • Client–server

    A GPU server generates the signal. A lightweight client (it needs only numpy and pyzmq) records it, on the same machine or across a network.

docs.title: Why software, and why a GPU
docs.text:
< $65K This approach: a GPU server and an open-source stack > $1M Commercial multi-channel, multi-band, phase-coherent RF simulators

Most verification work doesn't need real time. Accepting a slowdown (×10 or ×20) swaps expensive RF hardware for cheap compute time: a scenario that runs overnight delivers the same signal fidelity. The cost of each frame doesn't depend on how long the scenario is, and memory doesn't grow with it, so an hour-long run costs exactly 60 times a one-minute run. Where real time matters, small arrays already get there on one GPU. See the measurements →

Not there yet

Jammers are stationary: moving emitters are specified but not wired up. Noise and chirp jammers are accepted in emitter files but not yet rendered. Spoofers, pulsed jammers and multipath are specified but not implemented. Multi-GPU is designed but not built. Signals & interference lists exactly what is supported.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: How a scenario becomes samples: the signal model, the one design decision that makes it fast, how code timing stays exact at any sample rate, and the protocol between client and server.

docs.title: The signal
docs.text:
At antenna element m, on RF band b, the server produces

\[r_{m,b}[n] = \sum_{k=1}^{S} x_k^b\!\left(\frac{n}{F_s} - d_{k,m}[n]\right) \cdot e^{-j\,2\pi f_c^b\, d_{k,m}[n]} \cdot g_{k,m}\] Term \(x_k^b(t)\) Baseband of source k (satellite or jammer): code, navigation data, subcarrier \(d_{k,m}[n]\) Total delay from source k to element m: geometry + troposphere + ionosphere − satellite clock \(e^{-j2\pi f_c d}\) Carrier phase. Its rate of change is the Doppler. \(g_{k,m}\) Complex antenna gain: both patterns and the polarisation coupling

The delay does two things at once. It stretches and shifts the code (code Doppler), and it turns the carrier phase (carrier Doppler). The server outputs exactly this sum, with no noise. The client adds the \(w_{m,b}[n]\) term.

docs.title: Compute once, delay many
docs.text:
The key observation: the baseband depends only on the source, while the delay depends on the source and the element.

baseband x_k        depends on source k                 → computed once per frame
delay d_k,m         depends on (source, element)        → per pair
carrier phase       depends on (source, element, band)  → per triple
gain g_k,m          depends on (source, element)        → per pair

So the server builds each source's baseband once, then reads it out at every element with that element's delay, phase and gain. A new antenna element adds only a delayed read of buffers that already exist, so it costs far less than a new source.

docs.title: The delay
docs.text:
Geometry. The transmit position depends on the delay itself, so the light-time equation is solved iteratively: three fixed Newton iterations, vectorised on the GPU, to sub-picosecond precision. The Sagnac rotation is applied at every iteration. The element position is the receiver's position plus its lever arm rotated by the current attitude, \(\vec q_m = \vec q_\text{COM} + R(t)\,\vec l_m\).

Delay budget.

\[d = d_\text{geometric} + d_\text{tropo} + d_\text{iono}^{(b)} - d_\text{SV clock}\] Term Model Troposphere Saastamoinen zenith delay, Niell mapping function Ionosphere Klobuchar (IS-GPS-200), scaled by \(1/f_c^2\), so it differs per band Satellite clock Broadcast polynomial \(a_{f0} + a_{f1}\Delta t + a_{f2}\Delta t^2\)

Between snapshots. Delays are evaluated exactly every channel_period_s (1 ms) and interpolated to every sample with cubic Hermite polynomials, using both the delay and its rate at each snapshot. GNSS delays are smooth, so the error is \(O(T^4)\). The interpolation adds about three multiply-adds per sample.

Carrier phase in double precision. \(f_c \cdot d\) is about \(10^8\) cycles. Single precision would leave no usable digits in the fractional cycle that sets the phase. The phase is formed and reduced modulo one cycle in FP64, and only then cast to FP32 for the sine and cosine.

docs.title: Shaping, then delay
docs.text:
Every signal here is piecewise constant over segments: one chip, or 1/12 of a chip for the BOC(6,1) components of Galileo E1 and BeiDou B1C. Two steps turn segments into samples:

  1. Shape (once per source). The segment waveform is convolved with a fixed zero-phase low-pass filter \(h\) and evaluated exactly at each sample instant. A piecewise-constant waveform through \(h\) is a sum of \(h\)'s step responses, one per segment edge, so a single precomputed step-response table serves every signal and every rate. Segment indices come from exact integer arithmetic, never from floor() of a float.
  2. Delay (per source × element). A polyphase fractional-delay filter, with 256 phases of 24 taps, reads the shaped buffer at \(n - d_{k,m}[n]\,F_s\). Each output sample is an independent dot product, which is why all N samples of a frame can be computed in parallel.

The emitted spectrum is \(h\) times the delay filter's response. Both are defined in samples, so the sample rate sets the bandwidth:

Shaping \(h\) Delay filter Together Flat (≤ 0.001 dB) to 0.6 × Nyquist 0.6 × Nyquist 0.6 × Nyquist −6 dB at 0.8 × Nyquist 0.85 × Nyquist ≈ 0.78 × Nyquist Stopband ≤ −112 dB beyond Nyquist −29 dB at Nyquist Why shape before delaying? (changed 2026-10)

Earlier versions sampled the chips directly at each delayed instant. That moves every chip edge onto the sample grid and folds the rectangle's spectrum, which extends past \(F_s/2\), back into the band. The visible symptoms were a code-phase error of up to half a sample whenever the rate was a whole multiple of the chip rate, a small residual at fractional rates, and a ±0.5-sample sawtooth on BPSK jammers that was identical on every element. Shaping first removes all three. Measured code timing is now within 8 × 10⁻⁵ samples at every rate tested, and an independent analyser confirmed it. Whole-frame time stayed within measurement noise. More on Signal fidelity.

docs.title: GPU execution
docs.text:
Per band, per frame:

  • Shaping kernel. One thread per output sample, for a chunk of up to 16 sources. It evaluates the composite (code × data × secondary code × subcarrier) at segment centres and sums step responses. BPSK jammers that share a chip rate are shaped in the same launch.
  • Fleet polyphase kernel. A grid of (samples ⁄ 128) × elements. Each thread loops over every satellite and BPSK jammer, doing Hermite delay, a 24-tap FIR, the carrier and the gain, and accumulates in a register. There are no atomics, and each thread writes its sum once.
  • CW / FM jammer kernel. These have no edges, so their phase is evaluated directly at the delayed instant, which is exact. Jammers are tiled across thread blocks and reduced in shared memory.

Overlap. Geometry for frame N+1 runs on a CPU thread while the GPU renders frame N. Three CUDA streams (compute, host-to-device, device-to-host) and ping-pong output buffers keep the GPU fed, so throughput is max(geometry, render), not their sum.

Memory. The output buffer is bands × elements × samples × 8 bytes, allocated once. Basebands add one row per satellite per band. Even 3 bands × 16 elements × 250 sources at 50 MHz fits in about 3.2 GB. The cost that does grow is moving the output: see the transport bottleneck.

docs.title: Antenna arrays
docs.text: Each element is placed at the receiver position plus its lever arm, rotated by the body attitude at every 1 ms snapshot. The array's geometry therefore stays correct through manoeuvres. Gains use Jones vectors. The transmitter's field (RHCP for satellites, the emitter's pattern for jammers) is rotated into the element's frame and projected onto its pattern, giving polarisation coupling and, for CST patterns, angle-dependent group delay. All elements share one time base and one baseband, so the streams are phase-coherent by construction.

docs.title: Client–server protocol
docs.text:
ZeroMQ request/reply on one TCP port. Every request is JSON with a cmd and a client_id.

Command Does Replies INIT Claim the session and start preparing a scenario in the background. Carries the scenario text. OK, or BUSY STATUS Report progress. Allowed from any client. Current phase. At READY: fs, M, bands, sample_rates, carrier_freqs, active_sats, start_time_gps_sec, duration_s, frame_period_s, total_frames GENERATE Render the next n_frames JSON header + samples (format) TRUTH Ground truth for one satellite of the running session CSV text and a summary STOP Release the session and free the GPU OK SHUTDOWN Exit the server process OK UPLOAD_RINEX Store a navigation file in data/rinex/. Allowed from any client. OK 
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant S as Server
    C->>S: INIT (scenario text)
    S-->>C: OK, initialising in the background
    loop every 2 s
        C->>S: STATUS
        S-->>C: LOADING_CONFIG → PREPARING_EPHEMERIS → CALCULATING_VISIBILITY → INITIALIZING_GENERATOR → COMPILING_KERNELS
    end
    S-->>C: READY (fs, M, bands, satellites, …)
    loop until duration
        C->>S: GENERATE n_frames=10
        S-->>C: header + complex64 buffers
    end
    C->>S: TRUTH (optional)
    S-->>C: CSV
    C->>S: STOP
    S-->>C: OK (session released)

COMPILING_KERNELS includes a warm-up render of frame 0, which is why the stream starts at frame 1. A session left idle for 120 s is released automatically.

docs.title: Performance
docs.text: How fast it runs, what it scales with, and where the time actually goes, from measured runs on two Blackwell GPUs.

docs.title: Reading the numbers
docs.text:
The server works in frames of 100 ms of signal. A frame time under 100 ms is faster than real time. Above that, the slowdown is frame time / 100 ms: at 400 ms per frame, a 10-minute scenario takes 40 minutes.

Term GPU time Geometry, shaping, delay, jammers: everything until the frame is ready in GPU memory End-to-end GPU time plus the device-to-host copy and the transfer to the client

The cost of a frame doesn't depend on the scenario's length, and memory doesn't grow with it, so total run time is simply frames × frame time.

docs.title: The transport bottleneck
docs.text:
End-to-end time minus GPU time, on the RTX 5090:

Elements GPU Transport Transport share Data per frame 1 23 ms 18 ms 43% 59 MB 4 67 ms 92 ms 58% 236 MB 8 122 ms 184 ms 60% 472 MB 16 233 ms 352 ms 60% 945 MB

Every frame produces bands × elements × samples × 8 bytes. That volume, not the jammer count, sets the transport cost. At 16 elements the GPU is idle for most of each frame, waiting for the copy. For large arrays, a faster transport helps more than a faster GPU.

Same-machine clients

A client on the GPU host can take frames through shared memory (--transport shm), which skips the network serialisation. See Transport.

docs.title: Real-time envelope
docs.text:
The largest configurations whose GPU time stays under 100 ms on one RTX 5090, with 16 elements unless noted:

Signals Fits in real time GPS L1 up to 12.3 MHz with 20 jammers (82 ms) GPS L1 + L2 up to 6.1 MHz with 20 jammers (79 ms) GPS L1 + L2 + Galileo E1 up to 6.1 MHz with 20 jammers (96 ms) 4 elements, dual-band (CRPA) up to 24.6 MHz with 20 jammers (23 ms)

These are GPU times. For end-to-end real time on large arrays, the transport above also has to keep up.

docs.title: How it scales
docs.text:
Measured on the RTX PRO 4500, GPS L1 only, no jammers (March 2026 build):

1 element 4 elements 8 elements 16 elements GPU time at 6.1 MHz 8.8 ms 17.9 ms 28.1 ms 49.8 ms 6.1 MHz 12.3 MHz 24.6 MHz GPU time, 1 element 8.8 ms 12.5 ms 20.6 ms

GPU time grows more slowly than the workload at these sizes, because fixed per-frame costs dominate small configurations. Raw compute scales linearly with every dimension:

\[\text{FLOPs per frame} \approx \sum_\text{bands} N \cdot M \cdot \left(130\,S_\text{sat+BPSK} + 50\,S_\text{CW/FM}\right), \qquad N = F_s \cdot T_\text{frame}\]

Data volume scales the same way, and for large arrays it is usually the tighter limit.

What changed since these measurements

  • Shaping (2026-10). Building each baseband once per source left whole-frame time within measurement noise (−17% to +5% at 22 satellites, 1 and 16 elements, 12.3 and 24.6 MHz).
  • BPSK jammers (2026-10) now take the satellite path for exact code timing, so each costs about what a satellite costs. Measured: 50 BPSK emitters × 16 elements went from 301 to 373 ms per frame. The jammer rows above used BPSK jammers, so jammer-heavy cases are now somewhat slower than shown. CW and FM jammers are unchanged.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Problems grouped by where they show up. Most come down to three things: the GPU stack, the network path to port 5555, and files that exist on one machine but not the other.

docs.title: GPU and CUDA
docs.text: Symptom Cause and fix nvidia-smi: command not found No NVIDIA driver. Install 535 or newer and reboot. import cupy fails, or CUDA driver version is insufficient The driver is older than CUDA 12. Update the driver. cupy-cuda12x brings its own runtime, so the toolkit doesn't matter. no kernel image is available for execution on the device, or NVRTC errors on an RTX 50-series or Blackwell GPU The runtime is too old for compute capability 12.0. Install the CUDA 12.9 libraries and start the server with start_server.sh, which puts them on LD_LIBRARY_PATH. The first run sits at COMPILING_KERNELS for minutes Normal on a fresh install or after an update: CUDA kernels are compiling. They're cached in CUPY_CACHE_DIR, so the next run is fast. setup_env.sh fails with permission denied under /root You aren't root. Run ENV_ROOT="$HOME/.envs" bash scripts/setup_env.sh.

docs.title: Connecting
docs.text: Symptom Cause and fix Timeout waiting for GNSS server / Connection refused The server isn't running, the IP is wrong, or a firewall blocks 5555. On the server, check with ss -tlnp \| grep 5555 (Linux) or netstat -an \| findstr 5555 (Windows). Works on the server, not from a laptop The server is bound to 127.0.0.1 (GNSS_BIND), or the firewall allows only local traffic. Server is busy Another client holds the session. It's released when that client finishes, or after 120 s of inactivity. --status shows the server's state. OSError: [Errno 98/10048] Address already in use when starting Another process, often an earlier server, has the port. Stop it, or set GNSS_PORT. Remote client hangs or fails on the first frames The server is using the shm transport, which only works on the same machine. Start it with --transport zmq (the start scripts' default).

Download the named file and upload it, or put it in data/rinex/. emitter_file not found: … The emitter CSV is missing on the server. The scenario travels to the server; the files it points to don't. What lives where. An error loading the trajectory or a pattern Same cause: the path must exist on the server, relative to the server's working directory. Trajectory continuity error Two segments don't join within continuity_tolerance_m / _deg. Fix the CSV so that each segment ends where the next begins. See Emitter CSV. no satellite is above the elevation mask Lower elevation_mask_deg, or move start_epoch_utc or the position.

docs.title: Recording
docs.text: Symptom Cause and fix Fewer satellites than expected --max-sats (default 12) caps the whole run, in RINEX order, after any per-constellation max_sats. Raise it. A jammer has no visible effect Check its type: noise and chirp aren't rendered yet. Check its received power too: power_dbm is transmit power, and path loss over kilometres costs around 100 dB. An extra band appeared in the output A jammer's center_freq_hz is nearest to a band with no satellites, so that band was added for it. Empty or truncated .bin files The run was interrupted. The session is released on Ctrl+C, but the partial files remain. Record again. Disk filled up complex64 is 8 bytes per sample per stream. Use --format sc16 or sc8, a shorter duration_s, or a lower sample rate. Changing sample_rate_hz had no effect It's a server setting. Edit the server's config/simulator_params.yaml and restart the server.

docs.title: In the receiver
docs.text: Symptom Cause and fix PocketSDR: executable/script not found --pocketsdr must point at the PocketSDR root, which contains app/ or bin/. If the binaries aren't built, add --rx-type trk_py. No satellites tracked Check active_sats in recording.json, and that --signals names those constellations. A spectrum that looks mirrored, or acquisition failing on sc16/sc8 Integer formats invert Q. Conjugate the samples if your receiver expects the usual convention. Ranges off by tens of metres compared with truth Read truth at receiver time + 0.1 s. The recording starts one frame after the scenario start. A constant offset between pseudorange and truth That's the receiver's clock bias, which isn't part of the signal. Estimate it once and remove it. C/N0 doesn't match hardware It isn't meant to. The output has an ideal noise floor, so compare C/N0 between runs only.

docs.title: Still stuck
docs.text: Collect the server log (stdout, or journalctl -u gnss-server), the client output, the scenario YAML, the server's simulator_params.yaml and the output of --status. Together they almost always show which side failed.

docs.title: Signal fidelity
docs.text: A simulator is only as useful as your trust in what it emits. This page covers how the output is checked, what an independent instrument found, and what changed because of it.

docs.title: How the output is checked
docs.text:
Layer What it checks Unit tests (tier1) Code generators, navigation encoders, geometry, the trajectory and Hermite maths, filters Integration tests (tier2) Each constellation's full signal path, multi-band coherence, array phase across 6-DoF sweeps, antenna polarisation and group delay, atmosphere System tests (tier3) Whole-generator runs, including the client–server path Code timing at every rate For every band, the code phase recovered from the output is compared with an independent reference, at integer and fractional sample rates End-to-end truth The generated signal is compared with the ground-truth sidecar, across a frame boundary Navigation encoding Message structure, parity, CRC and FEC for GPS LNAV (against an open-source decoder), Galileo I/NAV, BeiDou B-CNAV1 and D1/D2, and GLONASS strings Golden regression Recorded reference outputs for GPS L1, L2 and Galileo E1. Any change to the signal fails until the bank is deliberately regenerated, and each regeneration is explained. A real receiver PocketSDR acquires and tracks the output. Its Doppler is scored against ground truth (results).

The test suite has about 70 modules. Run pytest -m tier1 for a fast pass, or pytest for everything.

docs.title: An independent instrument
docs.text:
gnss-vsa is a separate GNSS vector signal analyser that treats this simulator as a device under test, never as a reference. It acquires with PocketSDR, then measures with its own open-loop correlator, so that no tracking loop can smooth away the structure it is looking for.

Working with it changed how we read results:

  • Reproducing a number isn't confirming it. Two runs of the same code agreeing tells you nothing new. Three of the first four anomalies it reported turned out to be in the instrument, not the simulator. They were fixed upstream in gnss-vsa v0.2.0, and results from before and after that version aren't comparable.
  • A control has to differ from what it controls. Code timing is now checked against a reference that shares no code with the generator or with the instrument.

docs.title: What changed
docs.text:
The defects below were in the simulator. Each one was measured, traced to its cause, fixed, and re-measured after the fix.

Code timing within 8 × 10⁻⁵ samples at every rate; gnss-vsa's bench reads −0.0008 to +0.0004 samples. 2026-10-08 Every code was half a sample early whenever the rate was a whole multiple of the chip rate 12.2 m of code-phase bias at 12.276 MHz, on every satellite −0.5000 → +0.0000 samples 2026-10-08 Jammer carrier phase was interpolated in single precision and with zero rate between snapshots Phase noise that grew with range, and a carrier wobble for any moving geometry Both computed in double precision, from each snapshot's delay and rate 2026-10-08 The BPSK jammer restarted its chip sequence every frame A code discontinuity every 100 ms Continuous chips, timed from the scenario start 2026-10-08 A scenario naming a missing emitter file ran without jammers A clean-looking recording with no interference INIT fails and names the file 2026-10-08 GLONASS positions came out as NaN from a freshly parsed RINEX file No GLONASS signal from new navigation files Correct positions 2026-09-16 The Galileo E1-C pilot carried a 25-symbol secondary code that wasn't the ICD's A receiver wiping the standard CS25 couldn't integrate the pilot 380AD90, per ICD tables 22 and 24 2026-09-15 A chip index came from floor() of a rounded value at an exact tie Bursts of code-only jumps of up to 0.2 samples (5 m), on every satellite at once 7 events → 0

docs.title: Known limits
docs.text:
• C/N0 read off this output is not a carrier-to-noise density. The server emits no noise, and the client adds an ideal white floor with none of a real front end's noise figure or filtering. Compare C/N0 between runs, not against hardware.
  • Receivers that assume GPS-broadcast ionosphere (PocketSDR among them) leave a residual on other constellations, because the simulator applies one ionosphere to everything. That residual is correct physics and an expected result, not a simulator error.
  • BDGIM ionosphere is provisional and unvalidated. NeQuick-G isn't implemented.
  • Absolute pseudorange isn't claimed. See Ground truth.
  • Unrendered emitter types (noise and chirp) load silently. See Signals & interference.

docs.title: Deploy
docs.text:
Everything in deploy/ is for running the simulator as a service: one GPU server, and recording clients wherever the people are. This page helps you choose a layout. The pages after it walk through each part.

deploy/
├── server/
│   ├── start_server.sh / .bat   # launch the server with the right environment
│   ├── gnss-server.service      # systemd unit (Linux)
│   ├── start_telemetry.sh       # Prometheus + Grafana via docker compose
│   ├── prepare_rinex.py         # fetch a navigation file on a connected machine
│   └── requirements_server.txt  # pinned dependency list for mirror installs
└── client/
    ├── deploy_client.py         # the recording client
    ├── run_pocketsdr.py         # optional: track a recording with PocketSDR
    └── requirements_client.txt  # numpy, pyzmq

docs.title: Choose a layout
docs.text:
• One workstation

    Server and client on the same GPU machine. The simplest layout, and the fastest: frames can pass through shared memory with no network copy.

    For: individual developers, benchmarking.

    Quickstart

  • Shared GPU server

    One Linux GPU host runs the server as a service. Engineers record from their own laptops with a two-package client over TCP.

    For: teams, labs, test benches.

    GPU server · Recording client

  • Cloud GPU

    A rented GPU pod (RunPod, or any CUDA VM). Run the client on the pod and copy the results back, or tunnel port 5555 over SSH.

    For: occasional large runs, trying hardware before you buy it.

    Cloud notes

  • Air-gapped network

    No internet on the server. Packages come from an internal mirror, navigation files and updates by hand.

    For: classified or isolated labs.

    Air-gapped networks

docs.title: What lives where
docs.text:
The client sends only the scenario YAML. Everything else is read on the server, relative to the directory the server started in:

Item Lives on Notes Scenario YAML client Sent as text with each INIT, so you can edit it locally. simulator_params.yaml server Sample rates, carriers, frame timing, atmosphere models. Fixed when the server starts: restart it to change them. RINEX navigation files server Searched for in data/rinex/ and tests/data/. Clients can upload one. Emitter CSV, trajectory CSVs, antenna pattern files server Paths in the scenario are resolved on the server, so the files must exist there. Recordings client Written by the client wherever --output points.

A scenario that works locally can fail remotely

If your scenario names config/my_jammers.csv or a trajectory file, copy that file to the same relative path on the server. The scenario travels to the server; the files it points to don't.

docs.title: Ports
docs.text: Port Service Needed 5555/tcp Simulator (ZeroMQ request/reply) Always. Override with GNSS_PORT. 8000/tcp Server Prometheus metrics For monitoring 3000/tcp Grafana dashboards For monitoring 9090/tcp Prometheus UI For monitoring 9100, 9400/tcp Node and GPU (DCGM) exporters For monitoring, local to the host

docs.title: How sessions work
docs.text:
• One client at a time. The first client to send INIT owns the session. Others get BUSY until it sends STOP. STATUS and RINEX uploads are always answered.
  • Abandoned sessions expire. After 120 s with no requests from the owner, the server releases the session and frees the GPU. A crashed client doesn't lock the server for long.
  • The server outlives sessions. STOP releases the GPU and returns the server to IDLE. Only SHUTDOWN, Ctrl+C or the service manager stops the process.

The simulator port has no authentication

Anyone who can reach port 5555 can start runs, upload files into data/rinex/, and shut the server down. Open it only to trusted machines: a lab VLAN, a firewall allow-list or an SSH tunnel. Never expose it to the internet.

docs.title: Transport: zmq or shm
docs.text:
The server returns frames in one of two ways, chosen with --transport when it starts:

zmq shm Frames travel over the ZeroMQ socket through shared memory; only metadata on the socket Client location anywhere same machine only Used by start_server.sh / .bat (default) python -m gnss_sim.framework.server (default)

deploy_client.py detects which one the server uses, so the same command works with both. If clients connect from other machines, start the server with zmq, which the start scripts do.

docs.title: Cloud GPU
docs.text:
On a RunPod pod (or similar):

bash scripts/setup_env.sh          # first time only; keeps the env on fast local disk
source scripts/runpod_init.sh      # every session: CUDA 12.9 libs, paths, activation
./deploy/server/start_server.sh

You can reach the server in two ways:

  • Record on the pod, then copy the results back with scp or rsync. This is the fastest option, because 98 MB per second of signal per stream doesn't have to cross the internet live.
  • Tunnel: run ssh -N -L 5555:localhost:5555 <pod> on your machine, then deploy_client.py --host 127.0.0.1. The port stays private.

docs.title: Air-gapped networks
docs.text: The simulator needs no internet at run time. Four things have to be carried in by hand: Python packages, navigation files, Docker images if you want dashboards, and code updates.

docs.title: Python packages
docs.text:
deploy/server/requirements_server.txt is a flat, pinned list built for installs from a mirror with no build step. It mirrors pyproject.toml with its dev extras.

python3.11 -m venv .envs/gnss-sim
source .envs/gnss-sim/bin/activate
pip install -r deploy/server/requirements_server.txt \
    --index-url http://<artifactory-host>/artifactory/api/pypi/<pypi-remote>/simple \
    --trusted-host <artifactory-host>

Clients need only deploy/client/requirements_client.txt (numpy, pyzmq).

No mirror? Carry wheels on removable media

On a connected machine with the same OS, Python version and architecture:

pip download -r deploy/server/requirements_server.txt -d wheels/

On the target:

pip install --no-index --find-links wheels/ -r deploy/server/requirements_server.txt

cupy-cuda12x is large, a few hundred MB. Its wheel includes the CUDA runtime, so the target needs only the NVIDIA driver.

When you install from the pinned list, the package itself isn't installed. The start scripts set PYTHONPATH=src for you. If you run the server by hand, set it yourself.

docs.title: Navigation files
docs.text:
The server never goes online for ephemeris. For each scenario date:

  1. On a connected machine: python deploy/server/prepare_rinex.py --date 2026-01-15. It tries the requested day and up to four days before it.
  2. Carry the .rnx.gz across and put it in the server's data/rinex/, or upload it from a client inside the network: deploy_client.py --host <server> --upload-rinex <file>.

A navigation file covers one day for every constellation. A small library of dates covers most test plans.

docs.title: Monitoring stack images
docs.text:
The monitoring stack uses four public images. Save them on a connected machine:

docker pull prom/prometheus:v2.45.0 grafana/grafana:10.0.0 prom/node-exporter:v1.6.0 \
            nvcr.io/nvidia/k8s/dcgm-exporter:3.2.3-3.1.7-ubuntu20.04
docker save -o gnss-monitoring-images.tar prom/prometheus:v2.45.0 grafana/grafana:10.0.0 \
            prom/node-exporter:v1.6.0 nvcr.io/nvidia/k8s/dcgm-exporter:3.2.3-3.1.7-ubuntu20.04

Load them on the server with docker load -i gnss-monitoring-images.tar. Grafana's compose entry also asks to install two plugins (GF_INSTALL_PLUGINS). Offline, remove that line from docker-compose.yml, because the dashboards don't depend on those plugins.

Note

The map panels fetch OpenStreetMap tiles. Offline they show an empty background, and every other panel works.

docs.title: Update an offline copy
docs.text:
scripts/export_delta.py packages only what changed between two commits. Copy the package over a checkout that sits at the older commit, and the result is the newer one.

# On a connected machine, in a full clone:
python scripts/export_delta.py <commit-the-offline-copy-has> HEAD -o ../gnss-delta --zip

# Preview without writing anything:
python scripts/export_delta.py <old> HEAD -o ../gnss-delta --dry-run

The package keeps the repository tree and contains:

  • every added or modified file, at the new revision
  • DELETED_FILES.txt: paths to remove by hand, because copying files can't delete anything
  • DELTA_MANIFEST.json: both revisions and the full change list

On the offline machine, unpack it over the project root, delete the files listed in DELETED_FILES.txt, and restart the server. If pyproject.toml or requirements_server.txt changed, update the environment first.

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text: This site is static HTML. mkdocs build writes it to site/, which you can copy anywhere and open in a browser. Fonts and the MathJax script load from public CDNs. Offline, the pages fall back to system fonts and show equations as raw TeX.

docs.title: Recording client
docs.text: deploy_client.py connects to a server, sends your scenario, streams the signal to disk, and can bring back the ground truth. It needs Python and two packages: no GPU, no CUDA, no simulator install.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
Copy deploy/client/ to the machine. Those three files are all you need:

pip install -r requirements_client.txt     # numpy>=2.0, pyzmq
python deploy_client.py --host <server-ip> --status

With a mirror instead of the internet: add --index-url <your-pypi-mirror>/simple.

docs.title: Record
docs.text:
python deploy_client.py --host 10.0.0.5 \
    --scenario scenarios/crpa_test.yaml \
    --output recordings/crpa_run1 --truth

docs.title: Connect and send the scenario
docs.text: The client reads your scenario file locally and sends its text. Files it refers to, such as emitters, trajectories and patterns, must already exist on the server.

docs.title: Wait for READY
docs.text: The server loads the configuration and ephemeris, works out which satellites are visible, builds the generator and compiles kernels. The client polls every 2 s and prints each phase. If the server is in use, you get BUSY and the client exits.

docs.title: Stream
docs.text: Frames arrive in batches (--batch-size, default 10 × 100 ms). The client adds thermal noise and writes one file per band and antenna element.

docs.title: Truth, metadata, release
docs.text: With --truth, the client fetches the ground truth while it still holds the session, writes recording.json, and sends STOP. The session is released even after Ctrl+C or an error.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
Option Default --host (required) Server hostname or IP --port 5555 Server port --scenario (required to record) Scenario YAML on this machine --output ./recordings Output folder. Existing .bin files with the same names are overwritten. --format complex64 complex64, sc16 or sc8. See sample formats. --noise-dbm -174.0 Thermal noise density added to every stream (dBm/Hz) --max-sats 12 Cap on the number of satellites the server generates --batch-size 10 Frames per request --truth [SV] off Fetch ground truth after recording. Bare --truth takes the first generated satellite; --truth G05 picks one. --truth-rate-hz 10 Rows per second in the truth CSV (0 = every internal step) --status Print the server's status and exit --upload-rinex FILE Upload a navigation file to the server and exit

--max-sats caps the whole run

The server applies this cap across the whole run, on top of any per-constellation max_sats in the scenario. Satellites are kept in RINEX order, not by elevation. If you need every visible satellite of a big multi-constellation scenario, raise it.

docs.title: What you get
docs.text:
recordings/crpa_run1/
├── recording_L1_ant0.bin
├── recording_L1_ant1.bin       # one file per (band, element)
├── recording_L2_ant0.bin
├── recording_L2_ant1.bin
├── radial_truth_G05.csv        # only with --truth
└── recording.json

recording.json holds everything you need to read the samples back:

{
    "fs": 12276000.0,
    "bands": ["L1", "L2"],
    "n_ant": 2,
    "start_time_gps_sec": 1452546018.0,
    "duration_s": 60.0,
    "format": "complex64",
    "active_sats": ["G05", "G13", "G14", "G15", "G17"],
    "scenario": "scenarios/crpa_test.yaml",
    "server_host": "10.0.0.5",
    "recorded_at": "2026-10-09T08:30:00+00:00",
    "radial_truth": "radial_truth_G05.csv"
}

The Output files page covers the formats, the timing of the first sample and how to load the files.

docs.title: Upload a navigation file
docs.text:
If INIT fails with RINEX navigation file not found, the message names the file and its URL. Download it on any connected machine (or run prepare_rinex.py --date YYYY-MM-DD there), then:

python deploy_client.py --host 10.0.0.5 --upload-rinex BRDC00IGS_R_20260150000_01D_MN.rnx.gz

The server stores it in data/rinex/ and decompresses .gz files. You need to do this once per date, for all users.

docs.title: Check a recording with PocketSDR
docs.text:
run_pocketsdr.py turns a complex64 recording into PocketSDR's 2-bit format, writes the .tag file and runs the tracker:

python run_pocketsdr.py --input recordings/crpa_run1 --pocketsdr C:\PocketSDR
python run_pocketsdr.py --input recordings/crpa_run1 --pocketsdr C:\PocketSDR --antenna 1 --signals L1CA L2CM
python run_pocketsdr.py --input recordings/crpa_run1 --pocketsdr C:\PocketSDR --mode acq
Option Default --input (required) Recording folder (reads recording.json) --pocketsdr (required) PocketSDR root, containing app/ or bin/ --antenna 0 Element to process --signals from the bands PocketSDR signal names, for example L1CA L2CM L5I E1B E1C --mode trk trk (tracking) or acq (acquisition only) --rx-type from mode trk_py / acq_py uses PocketSDR's Python receiver if the binaries aren't built

The output is a tracking log with C/N0, Doppler and code phase for each satellite. With enough signal for navigation data, NMEA and RTCM files are written too.

A C/N0 read from this output is not a carrier-to-noise density

The server emits no noise. The client adds an ideal white floor, and the recording carries nothing of a real front end's noise figure or filtering. Use the tracker's C/N0 to compare runs with each other, not as an absolute figure.

docs.title: Monitoring
docs.text: The server publishes Prometheus metrics on port 8000 from the moment it starts. A ready-made Docker stack adds Prometheus, Grafana, and host and GPU exporters, with dashboards already provisioned. All of it is optional: the server runs the same without it.

docs.title: Start the stack
docs.text:
On the server, from the project root (needs Docker with Compose, and the NVIDIA Container Toolkit for the GPU exporter):

./deploy/server/start_telemetry.sh        # = docker compose up -d
Service Port What it is Grafana 3000 Dashboards. Anonymous access with the admin role, so keep it on the lab network. Prometheus 9090 Scrapes every second; data kept in ./prometheus_data node-exporter 9100 CPU, memory, disk, network dcgm-exporter 9400 GPU utilisation, memory, power, temperature

Prometheus reaches the simulator at host.docker.internal:8000. The targets are in config/prometheus.yml, the dashboards in config/grafana/provisioning/.

docs.title: Dashboards
docs.text: Dashboard Shows GNSS Telemetry Frame time split into GPU, gather and transport; real-time factor; throughput per band; satellites, jammers and antennas per band GNSS Navigation Receiver position on a map, speed and heading, satellite sky plot (elevation and azimuth), jammer locations Node Exporter Host resources DCGM Exporter GPU resources

docs.title: Server metrics
docs.text:
The ones you're most likely to chart:

Metric Type Meaning simulation_realtime_factor gauge Simulated seconds per wall-clock second. ≥ 1 means real time. processing_time_seconds summary Time to generate one batch gpu_processing_time_seconds summary GPU kernel time gather_time_seconds summary Device-to-host copy and gather transport_time_seconds summary Sending frames to the client frames_generated_total counter Frames since the server started gnss_sim_total_throughput_bytes_per_sec gauge Output data rate, all bands gnss_sim_band_throughput_bytes_per_sec{band} gauge Output data rate per band gnss_sim_band_sample_rate_hz{band} gauge Sample rate per band gnss_sim_band_satellites_count{band,constellation} gauge Satellites being generated gnss_sim_band_jammers_count{band} gauge Jammers being generated gnss_sim_total_antennas gauge Array size gnss_sim_sat_elevation_deg{sat_id}, …_azimuth_deg gauge Look angles per satellite simulation_rx_latitude_deg, …_longitude_deg, …_altitude_m, …_speed_mps, …_heading_deg gauge Receiver state simulation_time_utc_seconds gauge Current simulated time (Unix seconds)

To check that metrics are flowing without Grafana: curl -s http://<server>:8000/metrics | grep simulation_.

Where the time goes

With large arrays, transport_time_seconds often exceeds the GPU time: the output is bands × elements × samples × 8 bytes per frame, and moving it costs more than computing it. Performance has the numbers.

docs.title: GPU server
docs.text:
Set up a GPU host that serves recording clients over the network, from bare machine to a service that restarts itself.

Linux (recommended) Windows

docs.title: Check the driver
docs.text:
nvidia-smi        # expect Driver Version ≥ 535 and CUDA Version 12.x

If it's missing: sudo apt install -y nvidia-driver-535 && sudo reboot.

docs.title: Install Python 3.11+
docs.text:
Ubuntu 22.04 ships Python 3.10:

sudo add-apt-repository ppa:deadsnakes/ppa && sudo apt update
sudo apt install -y python3.11 python3.11-venv python3.11-dev

docs.title: Put the project in place
docs.text:
/opt/gnss-testbed-design is the path the systemd unit expects.

sudo git clone <repo-url> /opt/gnss-testbed-design
sudo chown -R $USER /opt/gnss-testbed-design
cd /opt/gnss-testbed-design

docs.title: Create the environment
docs.text:
python3.11 -m venv .envs/gnss-sim
source .envs/gnss-sim/bin/activate
pip install --upgrade pip
pip install -e .                     # or: pip install -r deploy/server/requirements_server.txt
python -c "import cupy as cp; print(cp.cuda.runtime.getDeviceCount(), 'GPU(s)')"

No internet on this host? See Air-gapped networks. On a Blackwell GPU, add the CUDA 12.9 libraries.

docs.title: Provide navigation files
docs.text:
The server needs a RINEX broadcast file for each scenario date, in data/rinex/:

python deploy/server/prepare_rinex.py --date 2026-01-15 --out data/rinex

Run that on any internet-connected machine and copy the file over. Clients can also upload one. If a file is missing, INIT fails with the exact filename and download URL.

docs.title: Review the engine parameters
docs.text: config/simulator_params.yaml applies to every client of this server: sample rate, carriers, frame timing, atmosphere. The shipped sample rate is 12.276 MHz. See Configuration.

docs.title: Open the firewall
docs.text:
sudo ufw allow from <lab-subnet> to any port 5555 proto tcp
# monitoring, if you use it:
sudo ufw allow from <lab-subnet> to any port 3000 proto tcp

Allow trusted machines only: the port has no authentication.

docs.title: Start it
docs.text:
From the project root:

./deploy/server/start_server.sh

Prometheus metrics exposed on port 8000
GNSS Simulator Server started on port 5555

From a client machine, check that you can reach it: python deploy_client.py --host <server-ip> --status should report "status": "IDLE".

docs.title: Driver, Python, project
docs.text:
1. Install the latest NVIDIA driver from nvidia.com/drivers, reboot, and check with nvidia-smi.
  2. Install Python 3.11+ from python.org and tick Add python.exe to PATH.
  3. Clone the project, for example to C:\gnss-testbed-design.

A separate CUDA Toolkit is optional: cupy-cuda12x bundles the runtime.

docs.title: Create the environment
docs.text:
cd C:\gnss-testbed-design
python -m venv .envs\gnss-sim
.envs\gnss-sim\Scripts\activate.bat
pip install -e .

docs.title: Navigation files and parameters
docs.text: Same as Linux: put RINEX files in data\rinex\ and review config\simulator_params.yaml.

docs.title: Open the firewall
docs.text:
In an administrator prompt:

netsh advfirewall firewall add rule name="GNSS Testbed Server" dir=in action=allow protocol=TCP localport=5555 remoteip=<lab-subnet>

docs.title: Start it
docs.text:
deploy\server\start_server.bat

The batch file activates .envs\gnss-sim, sets PYTHONPATH and the CuPy cache, and starts the server on port 5555 with the zmq transport.

docs.title: Start-script settings
docs.text:
start_server.sh reads three environment variables. The Windows script uses the defaults as fixed values.

Variable Default GNSS_PORT 5555 ZeroMQ port GNSS_BIND 0.0.0.0 Bind address. Use 127.0.0.1 to accept local clients or SSH tunnels only. GNSS_TRANSPORT zmq zmq for remote clients, shm for same-machine only (details)

Both scripts also set PYTHONPATH=src, CUPY_CACHE_DIR=experiments/simulation_results/.cupy_cache (compiled kernels persist across restarts) and CUPY_TF32=1. They always load config/simulator_params.yaml. To use another file, run the server directly:

python src/gnss_sim/framework/server.py --port 5555 --bind 0.0.0.0 \
    --transport zmq --params config/my_params.yaml

docs.title: Run as a service (systemd)
docs.text:
sudo useradd --system --home /opt/gnss-testbed-design gnss
sudo chown -R gnss /opt/gnss-testbed-design
sudo cp deploy/server/gnss-server.service /etc/systemd/system/
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable --now gnss-server

systemctl status gnss-server
journalctl -u gnss-server -f        # live log

The unit runs start_server.sh as user gnss, from /opt/gnss-testbed-design, and restarts the server 10 s after a failure. Change User= and the paths in the unit if your layout differs.

docs.title: Operate it
docs.text:
Task How See what it's doing deploy_client.py --host <ip> --status, or the dashboards Release a stuck session Wait 120 s (it expires on its own), or restart the service Stop the process systemctl stop gnss-server, Ctrl+C, or a client SHUTDOWN Change sample rate, carriers or atmosphere Edit config/simulator_params.yaml, then restart Update the code git pull (or apply a delta package), then restart Logs stdout/stderr, journalctl -u gnss-server under systemd

Kernel compile after updates

After an update or a cleared cache, the first INIT spends 1–3 minutes in COMPILING_KERNELS. Clients wait for it, because their status poll has no deadline. Run one short scenario after each deployment to warm the cache.

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text:
Record your first simulated GNSS signal on one machine, in about fifteen minutes. At the end you will have ten seconds of GPS L1 C/A as raw IQ, plus the ground truth it carries.

What you need

  • A Linux or Windows machine with an NVIDIA GPU: compute capability 7.0 or newer (RTX 20-series onwards), driver 535 or newer. Check with nvidia-smi.
  • Python 3.11+ and git. On Windows, Anaconda or Miniconda as well.
  • About 2 GB of free disk, and internet access once, to download a navigation file.

No GPU here? The recording client runs anywhere. See Deploy to use someone else's server.

Stop the server with Ctrl+C when you're done.

docs.title: Get the code and install it
docs.text:
Linux Windows 
git clone <repo-url> gnss-testbed-design
cd gnss-testbed-design
bash scripts/setup_env.sh
source .envs/gnss-sim/bin/activate

setup_env.sh creates a virtual environment, installs the simulator in editable mode with its dependencies (CuPy for CUDA 12 included), and builds PocketSDR into tools/ for later verification. It puts the environment in /root/.envs and links it as .envs.

Not running as root?

/root isn't writable for normal users. Choose another location: ENV_ROOT="$HOME/.envs" bash scripts/setup_env.sh

git clone <repo-url> gnss-testbed-design
cd gnss-testbed-design
scripts\setup_env.bat
conda activate gnss-sim

setup_env.bat creates the gnss-sim conda environment, installs the simulator in editable mode with its dependencies, and sets up PocketSDR in tools\.

Installing CuPy can take several minutes. Other ways to install, including one with no internet access, are on the Installation page.

docs.title: Check that Python can use the GPU
docs.text:
python -c "import cupy as cp; print(int((cp.arange(4) ** 2).sum()))"

You should see 14, which means a kernel ran on the GPU. A CUDA error here means the driver and CuPy don't match. See Troubleshooting.

docs.title: Download a navigation file
docs.text:
Satellite orbits come from a RINEX broadcast navigation file for the scenario's date. The server does not download one for you. Fetch it once into data/rinex/:

python deploy/server/prepare_rinex.py --date 2026-01-15 --out data/rinex

This saves BRDC00IGS_R_20260150000_01D_MN.rnx.gz. The server decompresses it on first use. When a scenario sets rinex_nav_file: null, the server looks in data/rinex/ for a file matching the scenario date (or up to five days earlier).

docs.title: Describe the scenario
docs.text:
Save this as config/my_first_scenario.yaml. It defines a static receiver in Tel Aviv, GPS L1 C/A from every satellite above 10°, one antenna, and ten seconds of signal.

config/my_first_scenario.yaml
scenario:
  start_epoch_utc: "2026-01-15T12:00:00Z"
  duration_s: 10.0
  rx_latitude: 32.08
  rx_longitude: 34.78
  rx_altitude_m: 50.0
  elevation_mask_deg: 10.0

  satellites:
    rinex_nav_file: null          # found in data/rinex/ by date
    constellations:
      GPS_L1:
        enabled: true
        common_power_dbm: -130.0

  antenna_array:
    elements:
      - id: ANT_1
        lever_arm: [0.0, 0.0, 0.0]
        orientation: [0.0, 0.0, 0.0]

The sample rate is not set here. It belongs to the server, in config/simulator_params.yaml, and ships at 12.276 MHz. Why the split →

docs.title: Start the server
docs.text:
Open a terminal in the repository root. The server resolves data/rinex/ and its output folder relative to the directory it starts in.

Linux Windows 
./deploy/server/start_server.sh

conda activate gnss-sim
set CUPY_TF32=1
python -m gnss_sim.framework.server --transport zmq --params config\simulator_params.yaml

When it's ready, it prints:

Prometheus metrics exposed on port 8000
GNSS Simulator Server started on port 5555

Leave it running. It's idle until a client connects.

docs.title: Record
docs.text:
In a second terminal, activate the environment again, then:

python deploy/client/deploy_client.py --host 127.0.0.1 \
    --scenario config/my_first_scenario.yaml \
    --output recordings/first --truth

The client sends your scenario to the server, waits while the server prepares, streams the frames to disk, then asks for the ground truth:

Sending INIT request to server...
Current Status: LOADING_CONFIG
Current Status: PREPARING_EPHEMERIS
Current Status: CALCULATING_VISIBILITY
Current Status: INITIALIZING_GENERATOR
Current Status: COMPILING_KERNELS
Current Status: READY
Server ready: fs=12.28 MHz, M=1 antennas, bands=['L1'], duration=10.0s (100 frames)
Progress: 100.0%
Recording complete.

Requesting ground truth from server...
  satellite  G05 on GPS_L1
  wrote      101 rows to recordings/first/radial_truth_G05.csv
Metadata saved to: recordings/first/recording.json
Session released successfully.

The first run is slow, and that's expected

COMPILING_KERNELS compiles the CUDA kernels just in time. The first run after installing can take 1–3 minutes. The kernels are then cached, and later runs reach READY in seconds.

docs.title: Look at what you recorded
docs.text:
recordings/first/
├── recording_L1_ant0.bin     # 982 MB: complex64 IQ, 12.276 MS/s, 10 s
├── recording.json            # sample rate, bands, satellites, GPS start time
└── radial_truth_G05.csv      # range, range rate, Doppler, delay per 0.1 s

Your satellite may not be G05. Bare --truth picks the first satellite the server generated.

A quick check in Python:

import json, numpy as np

meta = json.load(open("recordings/first/recording.json"))
fs = int(meta["fs"])
x = np.fromfile("recordings/first/recording_L1_ant0.bin", dtype=np.complex64, count=fs)  # first second

print(meta["active_sats"])
print("total power: %.1f dBm" % (10 * np.log10(np.mean(np.abs(x) ** 2)) + 30))

Expect about −103 dBm. That is the thermal noise the client adds (−174 dBm/Hz over 12.276 MHz). The satellites, at −130 dBm each, sit well below it, as they do at a real antenna. Samples are in units of √W, so |x|² is power in watts.

docs.title: Optional: check it with a receiver
docs.text:
The setup script built PocketSDR, an open-source multi-band receiver. Have it acquire and track the recording:

python deploy/client/run_pocketsdr.py --input recordings/first --pocketsdr tools/PocketSDR-master

It quantises the recording into PocketSDR's format, runs the tracker, and writes a tracking log with C/N0 and Doppler for each satellite. Compare the Doppler with radial_truth_G05.csv. The Ground truth page explains the 0.1 s offset you'll need to allow for.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: The simulator has two parts with very different needs. The server needs an NVIDIA GPU and the full Python stack. The recording client needs Python and two packages, and runs on any machine.

docs.title: Server
docs.text:
Minimum Recommended GPU NVIDIA, compute capability ≥ 7.0, 8 GB VRAM (RTX 2080 / T4 class) RTX 5090, RTX PRO 4500, or a datacenter GPU NVIDIA driver 535 (CUDA 12.x) latest CPU / RAM 4 cores / 16 GB 8+ cores / 32+ GB Disk 10 GB fast SSD sized for your recordings (see below) OS Ubuntu 22.04+ or Windows 10/11 Linux for long-running servers Python 3.11 3.12

VRAM is rarely the limit. Even the largest configuration we size for, with 3 bands, 16 elements, 250 sources and 50 MHz, needs about 3.2 GB. What drives the choice of GPU is speed. See Performance.

Recordings are big

A complex64 recording takes 8 bytes per sample, per band, per element. At 12.276 MHz that is about 98 MB per second of signal for one band and one antenna, so a 60 s, 4-element, dual-band run is about 47 GB. The client can write 16-bit or 2-bit samples instead (formats).

docs.title: Client
docs.text: Python 3.10+ with numpy>=2.0 and pyzmq. It needs no GPU, no CUDA and no copy of the simulator, only the deploy/client/ folder. See Recording client.

docs.title: Install the server
docs.text:
Setup script (recommended)Manual (venv + pip)Pinned list / internal mirror

The setup scripts create the environment, install the package in editable mode with its dev extras, and build PocketSDR into tools/ for signal verification.

Linux

bash scripts/setup_env.sh                 # once
source .envs/gnss-sim/bin/activate        # every new shell

The environment goes in /root/.envs/gnss-sim, or /workspace/.envs if /root doesn't exist, and is linked into the project as .envs. For a non-root user, set the location yourself: ENV_ROOT="$HOME/.envs" bash scripts/setup_env.sh.

Windows (needs Anaconda or Miniconda)

scripts\setup_env.bat
conda activate gnss-sim

python3.11 -m venv .envs/gnss-sim
source .envs/gnss-sim/bin/activate        # Windows: .envs\gnss-sim\Scripts\activate.bat
pip install --upgrade pip
pip install -e ".[dev]"

pyproject.toml is the single source of dependencies. CuPy comes in as cupy-cuda12x, which bundles its own CUDA runtime, so a separate CUDA Toolkit install is optional.

Keep the environment at .envs/gnss-sim. The server start scripts look for it there.

For machines that install from a package mirror with no build step:

python3.11 -m venv .envs/gnss-sim
source .envs/gnss-sim/bin/activate
pip install -r deploy/server/requirements_server.txt \
    --index-url <your-pypi-mirror>/simple
export PYTHONPATH="$PWD/src"              # the start scripts set this for you

The full offline procedure is in Air-gapped networks.

docs.title: Blackwell GPUs (RTX 50-series, RTX PRO Blackwell)
docs.text:
Compute capability 12.0 needs the CUDA 12.9 runtime libraries. Add them to the environment:

pip install --upgrade nvidia-cuda-runtime-cu12 nvidia-cuda-nvrtc-cu12

On Linux, deploy/server/start_server.sh puts these pip-installed libraries on LD_LIBRARY_PATH automatically. On RunPod, source scripts/runpod_init.sh at the start of each session does the upgrade, the library paths and the activation in one step.

docs.title: Check the install
docs.text:
# The GPU runs a kernel (prints 14)
python -c "import cupy as cp; print(int((cp.arange(4) ** 2).sum()))"

# The generator builds and renders a frame (mocked ephemeris, no RINEX needed)
pytest tests/test_gen_smoke.py -q

# The fast unit tier
pytest -m tier1 -q

The tests are grouped in three tiers: tier1 for fast unit tests, tier2 for integration tests and tier3 for full end-to-end runs. A bare pytest runs all of them, including the golden-signal regression.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Two YAML files drive every run. They are kept apart because different people own them and they change at different rates.

File Says Owned by Lives on Changes Scenario (for example config/scenario_config.yaml) What to simulate: when, where, which signals, which array, which jammers Test engineer Client; sent with each run Every run config/simulator_params.yaml How to simulate: sample rates, carriers, frame timing, filters, atmosphere Whoever runs the server Server; read at start-up Rarely

Any field you leave out takes its default. A scenario of ten lines, like the quickstart's, is complete.

docs.title: Annotated example
docs.text:
scenario.yaml
scenario:
  # ── When ──
  start_epoch_utc: "2026-01-15T08:00:00Z"   # ISO 8601, UTC
  duration_s: 60.0

  # ── Where: either a static position… ──
  rx_latitude: 32.08                        # WGS-84, degrees north
  rx_longitude: 34.78                       # degrees east
  rx_altitude_m: 50.0                       # metres above the ellipsoid
  rx_orientation: [0.0, 0.0, 0.0]           # yaw, pitch, roll in degrees
  # …or a trajectory, which overrides the static position
  # receiver_trajectory: "trajectories/flight.csv"

  elevation_mask_deg: 10.0

  # ── Which signals ──
  satellites:
    rinex_nav_file: null                    # null: found in data/rinex/ by date
    constellations:
      GPS_L1:
        enabled: true
        common_power_dbm: -130.0
        sv_power_offsets_db: { G05: +3.0, G13: -2.0 }
      GPS_L2:     { enabled: true,  common_power_dbm: -130.0 }
      GPS_L5:     { enabled: false, common_power_dbm: -125.0 }
      Galileo_E1: { enabled: true,  common_power_dbm: -127.0, max_sats: 6 }
      Beidou_B1I: { enabled: false, common_power_dbm: -130.0 }
      Beidou_B1C: { enabled: false, common_power_dbm: -130.0 }
      GLONASS_L1: { enabled: false, common_power_dbm: -131.0 }
      GLONASS_L2: { enabled: false, common_power_dbm: -131.0 }

  # ── Jammers (omit the section for none) ──
  interference:
    emitter_file: "config/jammers.csv"

  # ── Antenna array: one entry per element ──
  antenna_array:
    elements:
      - id: ANT_1
        lever_arm: [0.0, -0.05, 0.0]        # forward, right, down (metres)
        orientation: [0.0, 0.0, 0.0]        # yaw, pitch, roll (degrees)
        pattern: isotropic
      - id: ANT_2
        lever_arm: [0.0, 0.05, 0.0]
        orientation: [0.0, 0.0, 0.0]

docs.title: Time and place
docs.text: Field Default start_epoch_utc 2026-01-15T12:00:00Z Scenario start. Also selects the navigation file. duration_s 60.0 Length of the scenario. The run is duration_s / frame_period_s frames. rx_latitude, rx_longitude, rx_altitude_m Paris Static receiver position (WGS-84) rx_orientation [0, 0, 0] Static attitude: yaw, pitch, roll, in degrees, Z-Y-X receiver_trajectory null Path to a trajectory CSV (on the server). Overrides the static fields. elevation_mask_deg 10.0 Satellites below this elevation are not generated

docs.title: Satellites
docs.text:
Field Default rinex_nav_file null A path on the server, or null to search data/rinex/ and tests/data/ for the scenario date (up to five days earlier) constellations.<KEY>.enabled false (GPS_L1: true) Generate this signal …common_power_dbm -130.0 Received power for every satellite of this signal …sv_power_offsets_db {} Per-satellite adjustment in dB, added to the common power …max_sats all visible Keep at most this many satellites of this constellation, in RINEX order

Valid keys are GPS_L1, GPS_L2, GPS_L5, Galileo_E1, Beidou_B1I, Beidou_B1C, GLONASS_L1 and GLONASS_L2. The signals table gives each one's modulation, carrier and band.

Power is the total power of the signal at the antenna. A sample rate narrower than the signal emits proportionally less of it, as a real front end would.

docs.title: Antenna elements
docs.text:
Field Default id ANT_1 Name for the element lever_arm [0, 0, 0] Offset from the receiver reference point in body axes, forward-right-down, in metres orientation [0, 0, 0] Boresight relative to the body: yaw, pitch, roll in degrees pattern isotropic See below

pattern takes one of:

  • A built-in: isotropic (RHCP, unit gain), rhcp, lhcp, vpol, hpol, vdop or hdop (the last two are dipoles with sin θ gain).
  • A CST export: a path to a CST far-field .txt file on the server. Gain, polarisation and group delay are interpolated in angle.
  • Several CST exports by frequency: a map from frequency in Hz to file path. The pattern is interpolated between frequencies.
pattern:
  1227.6e6: patterns/ant_L2.txt
  1575.42e6: patterns/ant_L1.txt

Element m is generated for every enabled band, so the run writes bands × elements streams.

docs.title: Interference
docs.text: Field Default interference.emitter_file none Path to an emitter CSV (on the server). Leave it out for no jammers.

docs.title: Simulator parameters
docs.text:
config/simulator_params.yaml, as shipped:

config/simulator_params.yaml
simulator:
  frame_period_s: 100e-3          # one frame = 100 ms of signal
  channel_period_s: 1e-3          # geometry snapshot every 1 ms
  sample_rate_hz: 12.276e6        # all bands
  carrier_freq_hz:                # centre of each RF band's stream
    L1: 1575.42e6
    L2: 1227.60e6
    L5: 1176.45e6
    B1: 1561.098e6
    G1: 1602.0e6
    G2: 1246.0e6

  polyphase_L: 256                # delay step = 1/256 sample
  polyphase_taps: 24
  polyphase_beta: 8.0
  polyphase_cutoff_frac: 0.85

  atmosphere:
    iono_model: klobuchar         # klobuchar | bdgim | none
    tropo_model: saastamoinen     # saastamoinen | none
    klobuchar_source: gps         # gps (GPSA/GPSB) | bds (BDSA/BDSB)
    bdgim_alpha: null             # 9 coefficients in TECu, required for bdgim
    rel_humidity: 0.7

pipeline:
  enable_telemetry: true
  batch_size: 10

debug:
  freeze_nav_bit: false           # force navigation data to +1
  freeze_dynamics: false          # zero delay and Doppler
Field Default frame_period_s 0.1 Signal per frame, and the unit of client requests channel_period_s 0.001 Spacing of exact geometry evaluations. Delays between them use cubic Hermite interpolation. sample_rate_hz 24.552e6 (file: 12.276e6) Complex sample rate, as one number or a map per RF band carrier_freq_hz nominal per band Centre frequency of each RF band's output (L1, L2, L5, B1, G1, G2) polyphase_L 256 Fractional-delay resolution: 1/L sample. It sets only the table size, not the cost. polyphase_taps, _beta, _cutoff_frac 24, 8.0, 0.85 Delay filter design. Leave these alone unless you're changing the filter on purpose. atmosphere.iono_model klobuchar Ionosphere injected into the signal. bdgim is provisional. none gives a vacuum. atmosphere.tropo_model saastamoinen Troposphere. none turns it off. atmosphere.klobuchar_source gps Which broadcast coefficients from the RINEX header drive Klobuchar continuity_tolerance_m, _deg 0.001, 0.01 Largest jump allowed between trajectory segments

Use one sample rate with deploy_client.py

The server accepts a different rate per RF band, but the recording client records a single fs in recording.json and uses it to scale the noise. Keep sample_rate_hz a single number when you record with deploy_client.py.

docs.title: Choosing a sample rate
docs.text:
The sample rate is the bandwidth. Every signal is band-limited to it before it is delayed: flat to 0.6 × Nyquist, −6 dB at about 0.78 × Nyquist. Code timing is exact at any rate, so choose by the bandwidth you need, not to suit the chip rate.

sample_rate_hz Flat to Main lobes fully inside 6.138 MHz ±1.84 MHz GPS L1 C/A, L2C, GLONASS (centre channels) 12.276 MHz ±3.68 MHz All but L5 24.552 MHz ±7.37 MHz All but L5, including Galileo E1's BOC(6,1) lobes 40.92 MHz ±12.3 MHz All, including L5

A signal wider than the flat band is still generated, band-limited, and the server logs a warning. GLONASS FDMA channels sit between −3.94 and +3.38 MHz from 1602 MHz, so at 12.276 MHz the lowest channels reach past the flat band. Use 24.552 MHz if you need every channel flat.

Data volume and GPU time both grow linearly with the rate. See Performance.

docs.title: Timing rules
docs.text:
\[T_s \ll T_\text{channel} \le T_\text{frame}\]
  • \(T_\text{frame} / T_\text{channel}\) must be an integer.
  • \(T_\text{channel} \times F_s\) must be an integer, so that each snapshot covers a whole number of samples. At 1 ms, any rate that is a whole number of kHz works.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Complete scenarios for common jobs. Each one records with the same command; only the YAML changes.

python deploy/client/deploy_client.py --host <server> --scenario <file.yaml> --output recordings/<name>

All of them use the 2026-01-15 navigation file from the quickstart, and the server's shipped sample rate of 12.276 MHz unless noted.

docs.title: Dual-frequency GPS + Galileo
docs.text:
GPS L1 C/A, GPS L2C and Galileo E1 together: two RF bands, one element.

config/ex_multiband.yaml
scenario:
  start_epoch_utc: "2026-01-15T12:00:00Z"
  duration_s: 30.0
  rx_latitude: 32.08
  rx_longitude: 34.78
  rx_altitude_m: 50.0

  satellites:
    rinex_nav_file: null
    constellations:
      GPS_L1:     { enabled: true, common_power_dbm: -130.0 }
      GPS_L2:     { enabled: true, common_power_dbm: -130.0 }
      Galileo_E1: { enabled: true, common_power_dbm: -127.0 }

  antenna_array:
    elements:
      - { id: ANT_1, lever_arm: [0, 0, 0], orientation: [0, 0, 0] }

You get recording_L1_ant0.bin, which holds GPS L1 and Galileo E1 summed as at a real L1 front end, and recording_L2_ant0.bin. Track them with run_pocketsdr.py --signals L1CA E1B E1C L2CM.

Tip

Galileo E1's BOC(6,1) component sits at ±6.1 MHz. To keep it inside the flat passband, run the server at 24.552 MHz. See Choosing a sample rate.

docs.title: A moving receiver
docs.text:
A receiver driven by a trajectory file. The static position fields are ignored.

config/ex_dynamic.yaml
scenario:
  start_epoch_utc: "2026-01-15T08:00:00Z"
  duration_s: 60.0
  receiver_trajectory: "trajectories/accelerate_and_turn.csv"   # on the server

  satellites:
    rinex_nav_file: null
    constellations:
      GPS_L1: { enabled: true, common_power_dbm: -130.0 }

  antenna_array:
    elements:
      - { id: ANT_1, lever_arm: [0, 0, 0], orientation: [0, 0, 0] }

The trajectory format is 25 columns of position, attitude and their derivatives. Doppler now includes the receiver's own motion, and --truth reports it.

docs.title: A 4-element CRPA under jamming
docs.text:
A square array, 10 cm across, and three jammers. This is the case the simulator was built for: phase-coherent channels with known jammer directions, for null-steering and beamforming work.

config/ex_crpa.yaml
scenario:
  start_epoch_utc: "2026-01-15T12:00:00Z"
  duration_s: 30.0
  rx_latitude: 32.08
  rx_longitude: 34.78
  rx_altitude_m: 50.0

  satellites:
    rinex_nav_file: null
    constellations:
      GPS_L1: { enabled: true, common_power_dbm: -130.0 }

  interference:
    emitter_file: "config/jammers_l1.csv"                        # on the server

  antenna_array:
    elements:
      - { id: ANT_1, lever_arm: [0.0, -0.05, 0.0], orientation: [0, 0, 0] }   # left
      - { id: ANT_2, lever_arm: [0.0,  0.05, 0.0], orientation: [0, 0, 0] }   # right
      - { id: ANT_3, lever_arm: [0.05,  0.0, 0.0], orientation: [0, 0, 0] }   # forward
      - { id: ANT_4, lever_arm: [-0.05, 0.0, 0.0], orientation: [0, 0, 0] }   # aft
config/jammers_l1.csv
id,type,geometry_mode,latitude_deg,longitude_deg,altitude_m,power_dbm,center_freq_hz,freq_offset_hz,fm_deviation_hz,fm_period_s,bpsk_chip_rate,bpsk_seed
CW_NORTH,CW,STATIONARY_LLA,32.0900,34.7800,30.0,10.0,1575.42e6,2000.0,,,,
FM_EAST,FM,STATIONARY_LLA,32.0800,34.7900,30.0,20.0,1575.42e6,0.0,1.0e6,0.001,,
BPSK_SOUTH,BPSK,STATIONARY_LLA,32.0700,34.7800,30.0,0.0,1575.42e6,0.0,,,1.023e6,1234

You get four files, recording_L1_ant0.bin to ant3.bin. Every element has the same satellites and jammers, each with the phase its lever arm implies. The jammers are about 1 km away, so after path loss they arrive at about −87 dBm (CW), −76 dBm (FM) and −97 dBm (BPSK). That is 33–54 dB above the satellites, from three distinct directions. Read the files as a matrix:

X = np.stack([np.fromfile(f"recordings/crpa/recording_L1_ant{m}.bin", np.complex64, count=int(fs))
              for m in range(4)])           # 4 × N, ready for a spatial covariance
R = X @ X.conj().T / X.shape[1]

Co-located elements as a sanity check

Set every lever_arm to [0, 0, 0] and the four streams carry identical signals with independent noise. PocketSDR should then report C/N0 and Doppler that agree across elements to within a fraction of a dB-Hz and a fraction of a Hz.

docs.title: All four constellations
docs.text:
Every satellite system at once, with a cap to keep the run small.

config/ex_four_constellations.yaml
scenario:
  start_epoch_utc: "2026-01-15T12:00:00Z"
  duration_s: 30.0
  rx_latitude: 32.08
  rx_longitude: 34.78
  rx_altitude_m: 50.0

  satellites:
    rinex_nav_file: null
    constellations:
      GPS_L1:     { enabled: true, common_power_dbm: -130.0, max_sats: 8 }
      Galileo_E1: { enabled: true, common_power_dbm: -127.0, max_sats: 6 }
      Beidou_B1I: { enabled: true, common_power_dbm: -130.0, max_sats: 6 }
      GLONASS_L1: { enabled: true, common_power_dbm: -131.0, max_sats: 6 }

  antenna_array:
    elements:
      - { id: ANT_1, lever_arm: [0, 0, 0], orientation: [0, 0, 0] }

You get three RF bands: L1 (GPS and Galileo), B1 (BeiDou B1I at 1561.098 MHz) and G1 (GLONASS around 1602 MHz). Record with --max-sats 26 or higher. The client's default of 12 would trim this scenario's 26 satellites.

docs.title: An A/B pair: with and without atmosphere
docs.text:
To see what the atmosphere does to a receiver, record the same scenario twice. Run once with the shipped parameters, and once with the server started on a copy that switches the models off:

config/simulator_params_vacuum.yaml (changed lines)
simulator:
  atmosphere:
    iono_model: none
    tropo_model: none

python src/gnss_sim/framework/server.py --transport zmq --params config/simulator_params_vacuum.yaml

Everything else, including satellites, code and navigation data, is identical between the two recordings. The difference in the receiver's pseudoranges is the injected atmosphere, which you can compare with the tropo_s and iono_s columns of the ground truth.

docs.title: Ground truth
docs.text: The radial motion a recording actually carries, for one satellite: range, range rate, Doppler, delay and look angles over time. It comes from the simulator's own propagator, light-time solver and atmosphere models, so it describes the signal you have, not a second model of it.

docs.title: Two ways to get it
docs.text:
From the server (recommended)On the GPU host

Add --truth when you record:

python deploy_client.py --host <server> --scenario my.yaml --output rec --truth        # first generated satellite
python deploy_client.py --host <server> --scenario my.yaml --output rec --truth G05    # a specific one

The server computes it from the configuration it generated with and the satellite list it actually built. Nothing on your side can disagree with the recording: the parameters file, the satellite caps and the GPU all stay on the server. If you name a satellite that wasn't generated, you still get its geometry, plus a warning that lists the satellites that were.

scripts/radial_truth.py reads the same scenario and parameters the run used. Run it from the project root:

python scripts/radial_truth.py --scenario my.yaml --list          # which satellites a run generates
python scripts/radial_truth.py --scenario my.yaml --sv G05 --out truth_G05.csv

You must match the run by hand: use the server's simulator_params.yaml, and pass --max-sats 12 if the run was recorded with deploy_client.py's default cap. It also prints a cubic fit of range rate, if you'd rather have coefficients than a table.

docs.title: The CSV
docs.text:
Column Meaning t_rel_s Seconds from the scenario start t_gps_s GPS time range_m Geometric range, with light-time and Sagnac corrections range_rate_mps Its rate. Positive means receding. range_accel_mps2 Its second derivative, over a 1 s window doppler_hz What an ideal receiver observes. Negative when receding. delay_total_s Light time + troposphere + ionosphere − satellite clock sat_clock_bias_s, tropo_s, iono_s The individual terms elevation_deg, azimuth_deg Look angles from the receiver

Truth is computed at the array reference point, not per element; lever arms move it by centimetres. Rows come at 10 Hz by default (--truth-rate-hz, or --out-rate-hz for the script).

docs.title: Comparing against a receiver
docs.text:
Start with Doppler. It has no clock to remove and needs no calibration.

Shift by one frame

The recording starts at scenario time 0.1 s (why), so the receiver's timeline runs 0.1 s behind. Read truth at t + 0.1 s for a receiver epoch t. For Doppler the difference is tiny (about 0.06 Hz). For range it is tens of metres, enough to look like a real fault.

  • Absolute range includes your receiver's clock bias, which the simulator doesn't and can't know. Expect a constant offset between delay_total_s × c and the pseudorange. Measure it at the start and remove it.
  • Don't differentiate delay_total_s to get Doppler. Nine significant digits on a 70 ms delay turn into tens of Hz of staircase noise. Use doppler_hz, which is computed at full precision.
  • doppler_hz is not exactly −range rate × f/c. It also includes the satellite clock drift and the rate of change of the atmosphere, and both are in the file.
  • GLONASS carriers depend on the satellite. The truth uses each satellite's FDMA carrier.

docs.title: How well it's validated
docs.text:
Checked against PocketSDR tracking the generated signal:

Result Doppler, GPS L1 bias −0.044 Hz, RMS 0.348 Hz over 50 epochs Doppler, GLONASS L1 bias −0.031 Hz, RMS 0.150 Hz over 37 epochs Elevation and azimuth within 0.1° on 9 satellites Moving receiver 0.026 m/s against the expected line-of-sight speed

The remaining scatter is the receiver's own tracking noise. We stand behind the radial motion: Doppler, range rate and geometry. We make no claim about absolute pseudorange, for the clock reason above.

docs.title: Input files
docs.text:
Besides the two YAML files, a scenario can refer to a navigation file, a receiver trajectory, an emitter list and antenna patterns. All of them are read on the server.

Paths are resolved on the server

Relative paths are resolved against the server's working directory, normally the project root. When recording remotely, put these files on the server first. See What lives where.

docs.title: RINEX navigation file
docs.text:
Standard RINEX 2 or 3 broadcast navigation, mixed or single-constellation, such as the IGS daily BRDC00IGS_R_YYYYDDD0000_01D_MN.rnx. It supplies:

  • orbits and clock corrections for GPS, Galileo, BeiDou and GLONASS
  • the navigation message content each signal broadcasts
  • Klobuchar ionosphere coefficients, from the header

Set satellites.rinex_nav_file to a path, or to null to let the server search data/rinex/, then tests/data/, for the scenario date. If the date has no file, it tries up to four days earlier. .gz files are decompressed automatically.

The server never downloads a file. If none is found, INIT fails and names the file to fetch:

RINEX navigation file not found for date 2026-01-15. Please download from:
https://igs.bkg.bund.de/root_ftp/IGS/BRDC/2026/015/BRDC00IGS_R_20260150000_01D_MN.rnx.gz
Then upload it using: deploy_client.py --upload-rinex <file>

deploy/server/prepare_rinex.py --date YYYY-MM-DD does the download for you.

docs.title: Trajectory CSV
docs.text:
Receiver motion in six degrees of freedom, as a table of polynomial segments. Each row starts a segment that lasts until the next row's t_start. Set it with scenario.receiver_trajectory.

Columns Unit t_start s Segment start, from the scenario start x, y, z m ECEF position vx, vy, vz m/s ECEF velocity ax, ay, az m/s² ECEF acceleration jx, jy, jz m/s³ ECEF jerk yaw, pitch, roll ° Attitude (Z-Y-X) yaw_rate, pitch_rate, roll_rate °/s yaw_accel, pitch_accel, roll_accel °/s² yaw_jerk, pitch_jerk, roll_jerk °/s³

Within a segment that starts at \(t_0\), each axis evolves as

\[p(t) = p_0 + v_0\,(t - t_0) + \tfrac{1}{2}\,a_0\,(t - t_0)^2 + \tfrac{1}{6}\,j_0\,(t - t_0)^3\]
  • One row is a stationary receiver, or one moving at constant rates.
  • Past the last row, acceleration and jerk drop to zero and the receiver carries on at constant velocity.
  • Discontinuities between segments larger than continuity_tolerance_m / _deg are a fatal error at INIT. Make the trajectory continuous before you run it.

docs.title: Emitter CSV
docs.text:
One row per jammer. Set it with scenario.interference.emitter_file. Leave columns that don't apply to a row empty.

Defaults apply only to missing columns

A default below is used only when the column isn't in the file at all. An empty cell in a column that the row's type reads (for example a blank freq_offset_hz on a CW row) fails at INIT. Fill in every column your emitter types use.

docs.title: Columns for every emitter
docs.text:
Column Default id (required) Unique name type (required) CW, FM, BPSK, and also CHIRP, NARROWBAND_NOISE, BROADBAND_NOISE (which are rendered) geometry_mode (required) STATIONARY_LLA, the only mode implemented latitude_deg, longitude_deg, altitude_m (required) Location, WGS-84 power_dbm -100 Transmit power in dBm, into the emitter's antenna center_freq_hz 1575.42e6 Carrier. Also chooses the RF band: the nearest of L1, L2, L5, B1, G1, G2. pattern isotropic Emitter antenna: a built-in name or a CST file, as for elements yaw_deg, pitch_deg, roll_deg 0 Emitter antenna orientation in local north-east-down axes

Received power is computed, not given. Free-space loss at the band's carrier is applied over the true distance to the receiver:

\[P_\text{rx} = P_\text{tx} + G_\text{tx} + G_\text{rx} + 20\log_{10}\frac{\lambda}{4\pi d}\]

At L1 (\(\lambda\) = 0.19 m), 1 km costs 96.4 dB. A 1 W (30 dBm) jammer 1 km away arrives at about −66 dBm, which is 64 dB above a −130 dBm satellite.

Note

A jammer on a band with no satellites enabled adds that band to the output. For example, an L2 jammer in an L1-only scenario produces L2 files containing only the jammer. Emitters more than max(15 MHz, sample rate) from a band's centre are left out of that band. Within one band, every jammer currently uses the first jammer's antenna pattern.
