docs.title: Antenna patterns
docs.text:
An element's or an emitter's pattern can point to a CST far-field export (.txt). The simulator reads gain and phase for both polarisation components on a θ/φ grid, so it gets polarisation coupling and angle-dependent group delay, not just a gain. To model a pattern that changes with frequency, give one export per frequency:

pattern:
  1176.45e6: patterns/crpa_L5.txt
  1227.6e6:  patterns/crpa_L2.txt
  1575.42e6: patterns/crpa_L1.txt

Patterns are defined in the element's own frame: orientation turns that frame relative to the body, and the body's attitude turns it relative to the Earth.

docs.title: Output files
docs.text: What a recording contains, how to read it, and the frame stream underneath it, for anyone writing their own client.

docs.title: A recording
docs.text:
deploy_client.py writes one sample file per (RF band, antenna element) pair, plus metadata:

recording_<band>_ant<m>.bin    # e.g. recording_L1_ant0.bin, recording_L5_ant3.bin
recording.json
radial_truth_<SV>.csv          # with --truth

The bands are the RF bands that were generated (L1, L2, L5, B1, G1, G2), not the scenario keys. GPS L1, Galileo E1 and BeiDou B1C all end up in recording_L1_*.

docs.title: recording.json
docs.text:
Field fs Complex sample rate, Hz bands RF bands, in file order n_ant Number of antenna elements start_time_gps_sec GPS time of the scenario start (seconds since 1980-01-06). See the timing note below. duration_s Scenario duration format complex64, sc16 or sc8 active_sats Satellites actually generated, for example ["G05", "E11", "R03", "C21"] scenario, server_host, recorded_at Where it came from radial_truth Name of the truth CSV, or null

The first sample is 0.1 s after the scenario start

The server spends frame 0 warming up its kernels, so the stream starts at frame 1. Sample n of a recording is at

\[t_\text{GPS} = \texttt{start\_time\_gps\_sec} + T_\text{frame} + n / f_s\]

which is 0.1 s later than you might assume with the default 100 ms frames. A receiver's timeline therefore runs 0.1 s behind scenario time. Allow for it before you compare against ground truth.

docs.title: Sample formats
docs.text:
--format Each sample Bytes per sample Use it for complex64 float32 I, float32 Q 8 Full dynamic range. Required by run_pocketsdr.py. sc16 int16 I, int16 Q 4 Most SDR receivers; scaled so that σ = 8192 per component sc8 int8 I, int8 Q, values ±1 / ±3 2 2-bit receivers such as PocketSDR; threshold at 1σ

Samples are interleaved I₀ Q₀ I₁ Q₁ … with no header. The sc16 and sc8 scale is set from the first frame of element 0 of each band and then held fixed, so the AGC is frozen for the run.

sc16 and sc8 invert Q

The integer formats are written with Q negated, matching the spectral convention of MAX2771-based front ends, which PocketSDR expects. complex64 is written as is. If your receiver expects the usual convention, conjugate integer samples when you read them.

docs.title: Reading a recording
docs.text:
import json, numpy as np

rec = "recordings/run1"
meta = json.load(open(f"{rec}/recording.json"))
fs, fmt = meta["fs"], meta["format"]

def load(band, ant, seconds=None):
    path = f"{rec}/recording_{band}_ant{ant}.bin"
    n = -1 if seconds is None else int(seconds * fs)
    if fmt == "complex64":
        return np.fromfile(path, dtype=np.complex64, count=n)
    raw = np.fromfile(path, dtype=np.int16 if fmt == "sc16" else np.int8,
                      count=-1 if n < 0 else 2 * n).astype(np.float32)
    return raw[0::2] - 1j * raw[1::2]          # undo the Q inversion

x = load("L1", 0, seconds=1.0)
X = np.stack([load("L1", m, 1.0) for m in range(meta["n_ant"])])   # elements × samples

docs.title: Signal levels
docs.text: In complex64 files, samples are in units of √W: mean(|x|²) is power in watts at the antenna. The client adds white noise at --noise-dbm (−174 dBm/Hz by default) across the full sample rate. At 12.276 MHz the floor is −103.1 dBm, and a −130 dBm satellite sits about 27 dB below it, as at a real antenna.

docs.title: The frame stream
docs.text:
The server answers each GENERATE request with a JSON header, then the samples:

{
  "status": "OK",
  "n_frames": 10,
  "shape": [4, 10, 1227600],
  "bands": ["L1", "L2"],
  "first_frame_idx": 1,
  "t_start_scenario_s": 0.1,
  "scenario_start_gps_s": 1452546018.0,
  "total_gen_time_s": 0.84,
  "total_gpu_time_s": 0.41,
  "total_gather_time_s": 0.12
}

shape is (elements, frames, samples per frame). Then, with the zmq transport, one binary message part per band and frame, in the order L1/frame0, L1/frame1, …, L2/frame0, …. Each part is a C-ordered complex64 array of shape (elements, samples per frame). With the shm transport the header also carries shm_names, one shared-memory block per band holding the frames back to back, and no binary parts follow.

The output is full precision with no noise and no quantisation. Noise, AGC and quantisation are the client's job, so you can model your own front end. To write your own client, start from deploy/client/deploy_client.py: it is one file, and its recv_frames handles both transports.

docs.title: The developer client
docs.text:
experiments/rcv_pocketsdr_phase5.py is an all-in-one client for development on the GPU host. It records, quantises to PocketSDR's format (INT8X2 for one band, RAW8 for two, with a .tag file), runs PocketSDR on each element and prints a consistency table across the array:

--- Multi-Antenna Consistency Check ---
PRN 01: CN0 spread = 0.2 dB-Hz, Doppler spread = 0.1 Hz
PRN 03: CN0 spread = 0.1 dB-Hz, Doppler spread = 0.1 Hz

It connects to 127.0.0.1:5555 with the shm transport, so run it on the same machine as a server started with python -m gnss_sim.framework.server. --noise-seed makes a run bit-for-bit reproducible.

  • Signals on the same RF band share one stream. GPS L1, Galileo E1 and BeiDou B1C all land in the L1 files, as they would at a real L1 front end.
  • GLONASS channels are offset from the band centre. Each satellite sits at its FDMA channel's offset from the G1/G2 carrier.
  • Navigation data is real. It is encoded from the broadcast ephemeris in the RINEX file, with the parity, CRC and FEC each ICD specifies, so a receiver can decode it.
  • Every code is band-limited to the sample rate before it is delayed (why). Code timing is exact at any sample rate.

docs.title: Interference
docs.text:
Emitters are rows in an emitter CSV. Each has its own fixed location, transmit power, carrier and antenna pattern. Free-space path loss to the receiver is applied, and delay and Doppler are computed per antenna element, so an array sees each jammer from its true direction.

Jammers are stationary for now

geometry_mode: STATIONARY_LLA is the only geometry implemented. TRAJECTORY_FILE, for moving emitters, is in the interface but isn't wired up, so a row that uses it fails to load.

Type What it emits Status CW A single tone, optionally offset from the band centre Rendered FM A carrier swept by a triangle wave: deviation and period Rendered BPSK A pseudo-random BPSK spreading code at any chip rate, seeded and deterministic Rendered CHIRP A linear sweep, up, down or triangle Loads, not rendered NARROWBAND_NOISE Band-limited Gaussian noise Loads, not rendered BROADBAND_NOISE Wide Gaussian noise Loads, not rendered PULSED A gated version of another type Rejected at load SPOOFER GNSS replicas with controlled offsets Rejected at load

Loads, not rendered

A CHIRP or noise row parses and loads without error, but contributes nothing to the output. Don't count on these types for jamming-to-signal ratios until they are implemented.

BPSK emitters are shaped and delayed exactly like satellites, so each element sees its own sub-sample delay in the envelope. CW and FM have no edges, so they are computed directly at the delayed instant, which is exact for them.

docs.title: Channel effects
docs.text:
Effect Model Status Geometry Light-time solution with Sagnac correction, per satellite and element On Satellite clock Broadcast polynomial from the navigation file On Troposphere Saastamoinen zenith delay with the Niell mapping function On, can be switched off Ionosphere Klobuchar, scaled by 1/f² per carrier On, can be switched off Ionosphere, BDGIM BeiDou global model, with coefficients supplied by you Provisional Ionosphere, NeQuick-G Not implemented Antenna gain and polarisation Jones-vector coupling with built-in or CST patterns On Antenna group delay From CST patterns, by frequency and angle On Thermal noise White Gaussian, added by the client (−174 dBm/Hz by default) On Multipath Designed to reuse the direct path's baseband Not implemented

One ionosphere for every constellation

The ionosphere is a property of the medium, so a single model applies to every signal in the scenario. Klobuchar coefficients come from the RINEX header, which carries them whatever constellations you enable. A receiver that corrects with a different model, such as Galileo's NeQuick, is left with a residual. That residual is real; the simulator isn't wrong.
